transcript:
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in New York City, I'm Dua Hli Saikoutau.
Secretary of State Marco Rubio is now in Central Asia on another trip abroad
to meet with leaders of five Central Asian countries.
The trip is aimed at improving and promoting economic and regional security.
Ahead of the trip, he explained to reporters that the bill passed by Congress
to impose sanctions on Russia needed time to determine its effects.
I think when the bill was passed, one of the reasons the waivers were put in there
is understanding that they would need some period of time to study this,
given all the different things that are going on in the world right now,
including the pressure on global energy supplies that are happening
not just because of Iran and not just because of the Straits of Hormuz,
but increasingly because of the Houthis attacking Saudi Arabia.
President Trump signed an executive order to temporarily pause those sanctions
against Russia on Friday.
French President Emmanuel Macron addressed his nation after nationwide protests
led to scenes of destruction and violence across that country.
In Paris, Eleanor Beersley reports Macron began by condemning the violence.
Nothing explains it, nothing justifies it, nothing excuses it, he said.
Macron said the majority of protests were peaceful,
small, hardcore, far-left groups joined by "delinquents" came into cities to wreak havoc.
Those who destroyed will pay, those who pillaged will reimburse,
and those who wanted to bring down the Republic will have to answer for it, he said.
But Macron said those who committed violence should never be confused
with protesters with legitimate demands for better learning conditions
and worries over rising living costs.
His address is already being criticized by the right for not being tough enough.
One law and order politician has called for a state of emergency
and by the left for not proposing real solutions to the young people.
Eleanor Beersley in Pierre news, Paris.
President Trump continues his campaign rallies for GOP candidates this week.
Tomorrow he'll be in Kansas and with the midterm elections just about two weeks away,
Democratic candidates are raising more money than their Republican opponents.
In Pierre's moral ice and reports.
All through this election cycle, Republican campaign committees
and billionaire super PACs have been swamping their Democratic equivalents.
Elon Musk, for instance, has spent more than $150 million in Texas
to help the Republican Senate candidate there, Ken Paxton.
But according to the latest campaign finance filings,
Paxton's Democratic opponent, James Tallarico,
raised six times as much as Paxton himself this quarter.
Donations to individual candidates are usually a good proxy for voter enthusiasm
and this year the enthusiasm gap favors Democrats.
Democratic candidates in other key Senate races,
including Alaska, Ohio, Maine, Michigan and Iowa,
have also outraised their Republican opponents.
This is NPR News.
Advance polls closed late yesterday in Alberta,
ahead of tomorrow's referendum that may determine the future map of Canada.
As Dan Carpenschuck reports, people in Alberta are deciding
whether they want to stay in Canada or begin their process of separation.
Rallies have ramped up over the past week
with the most recent taking place in front of the Alberta legislature in Edmonton.
It was a final push to rally this separatist cause.
Hundreds of thousands of Albertans have already voted in advance polls
or cast their mail-in ballots.
Prime Minister Mark Carney, who grew up in Alberta,
attended forever Canadian rallies last week in Edmonton and Calgary,
urging people to vote in favor of Canada saying, quote,
"We are stronger together."
Albertans will vote on ten referendum questions,
the most notable whether to begin the process of separation.
If successful, that would mean another referendum, this one binding,
on whether they should go their own way as a country.
Surveys have shown that most Albertans want to stay in Canada,
but a significant number back in dependence.
For NPR News, I'm Dan Karpenschuck in Toronto.
In Bent, Oregon, a special needs teacher and a seven-year-old student
who were both wounded during Thursday's deadly shooting
at Silver Rail Elementary School remain hospitalized this weekend.
Oregon Public Broadcasting reports both are expected to recover.
Community members in the high desert area have been leaving flowers,
candles and stuffed animals at the school to remember the victims,
three children ages 5, 8 and 11, as well as their teacher,
25-year-old Megan Lambert.
The shooter, Griffin J. John II, was just 16 years old.
This is NPR News from New York.

topics.text: Secretary of State Marco Rubio travels to Central Asia to meet leaders of five countries
Trump pauses Russia sanctions via executive order, Rubio says waivers needed study time
French President Macron addresses nation after nationwide protests turn violent
Trump continues campaign rallies for GOP candidates ahead of midterm elections
Democratic Senate candidates outraise Republican opponents in key races including Texas and Alaska
Alberta holds advance polls ahead of referendum on separation from Canada
Special needs teacher and seven-year-old remain hospitalized after Oregon elementary school shooting
